content: Endometrial hyperplasia (EH) is a condition that can progress to endometrial cancer if left untreated, particularly when histologic nuclear atypia is present. EH develops due to prolonged exposure of the endometrium to unopposed estrogen, meaning estrogen is not counteracted by progesterone. Oral progestogens have been used to treat EH without atypia and, in some cases, EH with atypia, especially in women who wish to preserve fertility or are unable to undergo surgery. EH without atypia carries a low risk of progression to atypia or cancer, whereas EH with atypia involves structurally abnormal cells and has a higher risk of developing into cancer. However, oral progestogens are not always effective in reversing hyperplasia, can cause side effects, and require consistent patient adherence. The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) offers an alternative method of delivering progestogen and may have advantages over oral or other non-intrauterine progestogens. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of LNG-IUS in women with EH, both with and without atypia, compared to other treatments such as non-intrauterine progestogens, placebo, surgery, or no treatment. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, as well as trial registries and conference proceedings. The final search was completed in May 2020. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cross-over trials involving women with a histological diagnosis of EH, comparing LNG-IUS with other treatments. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The primary outcomes were regression of EH and adverse effects related to the LNG-IUS device, such as pelvic inflammatory disease, device expulsion, and uterine perforation. Secondary outcomes included rates of hysterectomy, hormone-related side effects (e.g., bleeding, pelvic pain, breast tenderness, ovarian cysts, weight gain, acne), treatment withdrawal due to adverse effects, patient satisfaction, and cost or resource use. The quality of evidence was assessed using GRADE methodology. Thirteen RCTs involving 1,657 women aged 22 to 75 years met the inclusion criteria. However, two studies lacked sufficient data for meta-analysis, so the quantitative analysis included 11 RCTs. The treatment duration in all trials was six months or less. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations including risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. LNG-IUS versus non-intrauterine progestogens: Regression of EH: The LNG-IUS likely improves regression of EH compared to non-intrauterine progestogens in the short term (up to six months), with an odds ratio (OR) of 2.94 (95% CI 2.10 to 4.13; moderate-quality evidence). This suggests that if 72% of women experience regression with non-intrauterine progestogens, 85% to 92% would experience regression with LNG-IUS. At long-term follow-up (12 months), LNG-IUS may also improve regression (OR 3.80, 95% CI 1.75 to 8.23; low-quality evidence). Adverse effects: There was insufficient evidence to determine device-related adverse effects, as only one study reported on device expulsion with inadequate data for analysis. Secondary outcomes: LNG-IUS may reduce the likelihood of hysterectomy (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.46; low-quality evidence) and treatment withdrawal due to hormone-related side effects (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.35; low-quality evidence). It may also improve patient satisfaction (OR 5.28, 95% CI 2.51 to 11.10; very low-quality evidence). However, LNG-IUS may be associated with more bleeding or spotting (OR 2.13, 95% CI 1.33 to 3.43) and less nausea (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.95). Data on mood swings, fatigue, and weight gain were limited but showed similar trends. There was insufficient evidence to assess cost or resource use. LNG-IUS versus no treatment: Regression of EH: One study showed that LNG-IUS is associated with regression of EH without atypia (OR 78.41, 95% CI 22.86 to 268.97; moderate-quality evidence) compared to no treatment. This study did not report on other outcomes. Conclusions: Moderate-quality evidence suggests that LNG-IUS treatment for three to six months is likely more effective than non-intrauterine progestogens in reversing EH in both the short term (up to six months) and long term (up to two years). However, adverse effects related to the device and hormones were poorly reported across studies. Low-quality evidence suggests that LNG-IUS may reduce the risk of hysterectomy, cause fewer withdrawals due to side effects, and improve patient satisfaction compared to non-intrauterine progestogens. It may also lead to more bleeding or spotting but less nausea. There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about device-related adverse effects, costs, or resource use.
